newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal Socialists may be Blair's trailblazer.
newsitem.headline: Portugal Socialists may be Blair's trailblazer.

text.p: If Britain's opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair is looking for a precedent for his bid to oust a long-ruling incumbent in next month's vote, Portugal's Socialists can offer one.
For Portugal, Britain's high-decibel campaigning increasingly sounds like an echo of its own elections 18 months ago -- right down to the likely outcome.
In Lisbon, a revitalised and reformed Socialist Party defeated a tired centre-right administration that had dominated Portuguese politics for the best part of two decades.
And it did so by offering change but not too much.
If the opinion polls are right, Blair should become Britain's next prime minister after elections on May 1, and end 18 years of Conservative Party rule.

Like Britain's Labour Party, Portugal's Socialists promised not to raise taxes as they set out to reassure the country's burgeoning middle classes that they could be trusted with running the economy efficiently.

Like Blair, party leader Antonio Guterres, now Prime Minister, also made education his number one social priority while quietly ditching most of his party's traditional Socialist rhetoric in the name of moderation and responsibility.
"The Labour Party and Portugal's Socialists are similar in the way that they have sought to occupy the political middle ground," said one European diplomat in Lisbon.
"They both needed to show that they could be trusted once again," he added.

In Portuguese minds, the Socialists were long associated with the turbulence of the late 1970s and early 1980s when the country took a decade to settle down after the 1974 armed forces' revolt that ended 40 years of right-wing dictatorship.
As in Britain, where the 1970s were years of industrial turmoil, the centre right became associated with order and social stability.
Britain had Margaret Thatcher, while Portugal had Anibal Cavaco Silva, a charismatic former university professor who led the country for a decade from 1985 until the elections in October 1995.
"It is phase that all centre-left political parties have been going through," said political analyst Carlos Magno.

"The line adopted by Blair and Guterres has been similar. Both concentrated their (electoral) attacks on the way power was used by the government rather than on the policies of their centre-right opponents," he said.
In the case of the British and Portuguese Socialist leaders, they have one further element in common. Both are practising Christians at the head of political parties with strong laical traditions.

But if the road to power, assuming, of course, Blair wins, may take a similar route, the performance of the Portuguese Socialists in office may not provide clues to life under a Labour government, political analysts say.

For a start, unlike the British party, the Portuguese Socialists are fervently pro-Europe and the Guterres government has effectively staked its political credibility on the country making the grade for the single currency in 1999.

So far the omens are good. From being a rank outsider a few months ago, Portugal has emerged as a serious candidate to take its place alongside European giants Germany and France at the launch of monetary union.
The explanation is a dedication to budgetary and financial discipline that even the Socialists's conservative Social Democrat opponents are hard pressed to fault.

An improving economy, an initially lacklustre opposition and public approval of the more conciliatory, less autocratic, style of government adopted by Guterres, ensured the Socialists a lengthy honeymoon with public opinion.
But there are signs -- worrying for Guterres -- that the public mood is beginning to swing.

Polls still show him outscoring his main opponent, Social Democrat leader Marcelo Rebelo de Sousa, but some well-publicised rows within his party and a sense that the government is postponing difficult decisions have begun to take their toll.

Guterres, like Blair, fought a tough political battle within his party after taking over the leadership in 1992 to strip it of the ideological trappings which he felt would bar it ever returning to power.

But while the policies have gone, many of the personalities remain and it is the old Socialist stalwarts, the so-called 'historicals', who can still cause Guterres some political embarrassment, political analysts say.
It is a lesson Blair would do well not to forget, they add.
The 'historicals' were behind a highly public row over liberalising abortion, which Guterres' opposes, and squabbling over a behind-the-scenes deal with the opposition on constitutional reforms.
